---



A drawing becomes far more informative when its colors and sizes carry data. Coloring nodes by
community shows how a network divides, sizing them by centrality shows where its influence lies,
and coloring edges by whether they stay within a group or cross between groups shows how the
groups are linked. These *aesthetic mappings* translate node attributes into visual properties.

`plot()` has three of them: `color_by=` for node colors, `size_by=` for node sizes, and
`edge_color_by=` for edge colors. Each takes the name of a node attribute, so anything stored on
the nodes can drive the drawing, whether it came with the data, was set with `set_node_attrs()`, or
was computed by an analysis method such as `pagerank()` or `cmty_louvain()`. This page shows how to
use them, how to choose a palette, and how to prepare visual attributes for the interactive views.

## Coloring nodes by category

`color_by=` gives each distinct value of an attribute its own color. The karate club records which
faction each member joined when the club split:

::: {#3c972def .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.plot(color_by="faction", label_by="label", seed=1)
```

<script>
(function(){
  var tip=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('#ec-tooltip-1');
  var svg=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('svg');
  if(!svg||!tip) return;
  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');
    if(!raw) return;
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];
      if(typeof v==='number'&&!Number.isInteger(v)) v=v.toFixed(4);
      h+='<div><b>'+k+'</b>: '+v+'</div>';
    }
    if(!h) return;
    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  }
  svg.addEventListener('mouseover',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge')) show(t,ev);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mousemove',function(ev){
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mouseout',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge'))
      tip.style.display='none';
  });
})();
</script>

:::


The two factions occupy the two sides of the drawing, as expected from a network that split along
its weakest links. Edges between two members of the same faction take the faction's color, while
edges between the factions keep the neutral edge color, so the few ties that cross the divide stand
out as the gray lines in the middle.

The mapping is categorical: each distinct value gets the next color of the palette, in the order
in which the values are first met among the nodes. Nodes that lack the attribute are grouped
together and get a color of their own. Any kind of value works, including strings, integers, and
booleans. The `role` attribute picks out the club's two leaders:

(function(){
  var tip=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('#ec-tooltip-2');
  var svg=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('svg');
  if(!svg||!tip) return;
  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');
    if(!raw) return;
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];
      if(typeof v==='number'&&!Number.isInteger(v)) v=v.toFixed(4);
      h+='<div><b>'+k+'</b>: '+v+'</div>';
    }
    if(!h) return;
    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  }
  svg.addEventListener('mouseover',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge')) show(t,ev);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mousemove',function(ev){
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mouseout',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge'))
      tip.style.display='none';
  });
})();
</script>

### Coloring by computed results

Analysis methods that assign nodes to groups store their results as node attributes, which
`color_by=` can then use directly. The most common case is community detection. Running
[`cmty_louvain()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_louvain.qmd) on the dolphin network stores each animal's
community in the `cmty_louvain` attribute:

::: {#408a1522 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
dolphins = ec.dolphins()
dolphins.cmty_louvain()
dolphins.plot(color_by="cmty_louvain", palette="Set2", show_labels=False, node_size=7, seed=1)
```

(function(){

  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');

    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];

      h+='<div><b>'+k+'</b>: '+v+'</div>';

    if(!h) return;
    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  }
  svg.addEventListener('mouseover',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge')) show(t,ev);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mousemove',function(ev){
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';

    var t=ev.target;

  });
})();

The Louvain method finds five communities. The two large groups of the population, at the top
and the bottom of the drawing, correspond to the two main communities the researchers observed,
and the method splits the lower group further into smaller circles of associates. Plotting a
community detection result like this is the quickest check of whether the groups it found make
sense. [Community detection](communities.qmd) describes the methods.

### Deriving categories with Polars

When the categories to show aren't stored on the graph, they can be computed from the node table
with Polars and written back with `set_node_attrs()`. Suppose the question is which members were
friends with both leaders, and so stood between the two camps:

::: {#047107fc .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
both_leaders = set(karate.get_neighbors(1)) & set(karate.get_neighbors(34))

positions = karate.get_node_df().select(
    "id",
    pl.when(pl.col("role") != "Member")
    .then(pl.col("role"))
    .when(pl.col("id").is_in(list(both_leaders)))
    .then(pl.lit("Friend of both"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("Other"))
    .alias("position"),
)
karate.set_node_attrs("position", dict(positions.iter_rows()))
karate.plot(color_by="position", label_by="label", seed=1)
```

(function(){

  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');
    if(!raw) return;
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];
      if(typeof v==='number'&&!Number.isInteger(v)) v=v.toFixed(4);

    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();

administrator, and they sit in the middle of the drawing, between the two camps. The pattern of a
Polars expression followed by `set_node_attrs()` works for any categorization, such as binning a
numeric score into "low", "medium", and "high"; [Node and edge data](node-and-edge-data.qmd)
describes it in more detail.

## Palettes

`palette=` chooses the colors that `color_by=` and `edge_color_by=` use. The default is
`"tableau"`, and [`list_palettes()`](../reference/list_palettes.qmd) lists the others:

The palettes fall into three families:

- **qualitative** palettes, such as `"tableau"`, `"Set1"`, `"Set2"`, `"Dark2"`, `"Paired"`, and
  `"Accent"`, have colors that are distinct but not ordered, which suits categories such as
  communities, types, or factions
- **sequential** palettes, such as `"Blues"`, `"Greens"`, `"YlOrRd"`, and the perceptually uniform
  `"viridis"`, `"magma"`, `"inferno"`, `"plasma"`, and `"cividis"`, run from light to dark
- **diverging** palettes, such as `"RdBu"`, `"PiYG"`, and `"Spectral"`, run between two contrasting
  colors through a neutral middle

The `get_palette()` function returns the colors of a palette as hex strings, which is useful for
matching other figures or legends to a plot:

::: {#1c1c012a .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
colors.get_palette("Set2")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7}
```
['#66c2a5',
 '#fc8d62',
 '#8da0cb',
 '#e78ac3',
 '#a6d854',
 '#ffd92f',
 '#e5c494',
 '#b3b3b3']
```
:::
:::


Most qualitative palettes have 8 to 12 colors, and when an attribute has more distinct values than
the palette has colors, the colors are reused from the start, so two groups can end up with the
same color. `"Paired"` and `"Set3"` have the most colors, twelve each. For attributes with many
values, it is usually better to color only the few largest groups and merge the rest into an
"other" category.

Since `color_by=` assigns colors in order of first appearance rather than in sorted order of the
values, a sequential palette does not produce a gradient that follows the values. For ordered
categories, choose a qualitative palette, and for numeric values, use `size_by=`, described next.
The colorblind-safe palettes include `"Dark2"`, `"Set2"`, `"Paired"`, and the viridis family.

## Sizing nodes by value

`size_by=` maps a numeric attribute to the node radius. The values are scaled linearly so that the
smallest value gets half the base `node_size=` and the largest twice it, and nodes with a missing
or non-numeric value keep the base size. `"degree"` is always available. Sizing by
[`pagerank()`](../reference/Graph.pagerank.qmd), with the factions as colors:

::: {#33185d14 .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
karate.pagerank()
karate.plot(color_by="faction", size_by="pagerank", label_by="label", seed=1)
```

(function(){

  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');
    if(!raw) return;
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];

The administrator, `"33"`, and the instructor, `"0"`, are by far the largest nodes, followed by the
members closest to them, such as `"32"`, `"2"`, and `"1"`. Since the scale runs from the smallest
value to the largest, differences in size reflect differences in value, but not their ratios: a
node twice the size of another doesn't have twice the score. A single extreme value
compresses all the other nodes toward the small end, which is often the case for betweenness, where
a few bridges have most of the total.

## Coloring edges by group

`edge_color_by=` colors the edges by the groups of their endpoints, independently of the node
colors. An edge whose two endpoints share a value gets that group's color, and an edge between two
different groups gets the `cross_community_color=`, a muted red by default. This turns the edges
between groups into the focus of the drawing:

::: {#e321d8fe .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
karate.plot(
    color_by="faction",
    edge_color_by="faction",
    cross_community_color="crimson",
    edge_opacity=0.6,
    label_by="label",
    seed=1,
)
```

(function(){
  var tip=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('#ec-tooltip-6');
  var svg=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('svg');
  if(!svg||!tip) return;
  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');
    if(!raw) return;
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];
      if(typeof v==='number'&&!Number.isInteger(v)) v=v.toFixed(4);
      h+='<div><b>'+k+'</b>: '+v+'</div>';
    }
    if(!h) return;
    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  }
  svg.addEventListener('mouseover',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge')) show(t,ev);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mousemove',function(ev){
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mouseout',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge'))
      tip.style.display='none';
  });
})();
</script>

The ten friendships that crossed the divide are drawn in crimson. Half of them involve a single
member, `"2"`, who was friends with five members of the administrator's faction, and most of the
rest involve the instructor or the members who were friends with both leaders. Raising
`edge_opacity=` from its default of 0.4 makes the edge colors easier to see. `edge_color_by=` can
use a different attribute from `color_by=`, for example nodes colored by a detected community and
edges colored by the known factions, which shows where the two partitions disagree.
`cross_community_color=` takes any color that SVG understands, a name such as `"crimson"` or a hex
code such as `"#999999"`.

## Putting it together

The mappings combine freely, and they work with both themes. The *Les Misérables* network, with
nodes colored by their [Leiden](../reference/Graph.cmty_leiden.qmd) community and sized by
[betweenness](../reference/Graph.betweenness_centrality.qmd), on a dark background:

::: {#9a068a5b .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
miserables = ec.les_miserables()
miserables.cmty_leiden().betweenness_centrality()
miserables.plot(
    theme="dark",
    color_by="cmty_leiden",
    size_by="betweenness_centrality",
    palette="Set3",
    show_labels=False,
    seed=2,
)
```

The largest node by far is Valjean, who connects almost every part of the novel. The other large
nodes, Gavroche, Javert, Myriel, Thénardier, and Fantine, are the characters who link a storyline
to the rest: Myriel, for example, is the only link between the fan of minor characters on the left
and the rest of the cast. The drawing shows in
one picture both how the cast divides into storylines and which characters hold them together.

## Visual attributes for the interactive views

`plot()` computes its colors and sizes from the mappings at drawing time. The interactive views of
[Interactive widgets](interactive.qmd) work differently: they read visual properties stored on
the nodes themselves, a `color` attribute holding a color string and a `size` attribute holding a
number. Two methods prepare these attributes.

[`colorize_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.colorize_node_attrs.qmd) maps a categorical attribute
to colors and writes them to the `color` attribute. Unlike `color_by=`, it sorts the distinct
values before assigning colors, so the same values always get the same colors.
[`rescale_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.rescale_node_attrs.qmd) maps a numeric attribute
linearly onto a range and writes the results to the `size` attribute:

::: {#9a19f8f1 .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
karate.colorize_node_attrs("faction", palette="Set2")
karate.rescale_node_attrs("pagerank", range=[10, 40])
karate.get_node_df().select("label", "faction", "color", "pagerank", "size").head(4)
```

Both methods modify the graph in place, and `node_attr_to=` writes to an attribute other than
`color` or `size`. `colorize_node_attrs()` also accepts a list of colors instead of a palette name,
and `alpha=` adds transparency. Both record the mapping on the graph, and
[`describe()`](../reference/Graph.describe.qmd) lists the recorded mappings under "Node
aesthetics", which documents how a figure was made. The stored colors are used by
[`plot_vis()`](interactive.qmd) and the graph widget; `plot()` itself ignores them and uses its
own mappings.

## Summary

| Argument or method | Maps | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `color_by=` | a categorical node attribute to node colors | edges within a group take its color |
| `palette=` | the colors used by `color_by=` and `edge_color_by=` | see `list_palettes()` |
| `size_by=` | a numeric node attribute, or `"degree"`, to node size | half to twice `node_size=` |
| `edge_color_by=` | a node attribute to edge colors, by endpoint group | cross-group edges get `cross_community_color=` |
| `edge_opacity=` | edge transparency | default `0.4` |
| `colorize_node_attrs()` | a categorical attribute to stored `color` values | for the interactive views |
| `rescale_node_attrs()` | a numeric attribute to stored `size` values | for the interactive views |
